prompt:
A densely annotated editorial infographic plate, drawn by hand in confident ink
line with light watercolour and gouache wash on bright warm-white paper.
Contour line varies in weight and is charcoal near-black. Dimensional but not
photographic: restrained hatching, subtle texture, believable volume, selective
shadow, clean uncluttered background. Every material reads as itself — dull grey
lead, unglazed earthenware, weathered timber, damp fibrous bark — and materials
that differ in the explanation look visibly different. Quiet palette of stone,
clay, wood, and metal tones over the warm-white ground, with one or two
desaturated accents that each keep a single meaning throughout the plate.
Contemporary editorial typography: one calm display face for the title, one
highly legible face for the many small labels, sentence case, crisply printed
and correctly spelled. Annotation is dense and disciplined — leader lines,
brackets, dimension marks, magnified inset circles, small side studies — laid
out so no two leaders cross. Asymmetric composition with about a quarter of the
page left quiet. Modern printing on clean stock: fresh, crisp, and unaged. The
only lettering anywhere on the plate is the title, the deck, the labels, and the
short notes. The words hero, drawing, figure, plate, inset, zone, band, strip,
trio, column, and cutaway describe the construction of the page and are never
lettered onto it, alone or in a phrase: no headings that name parts of the
layout, no percentages or
proportions of the page, no tags in brackets after a label or note, no sentence
describing the drawing or explaining what the reader is meant to see, no
signature, monogram, date, watermark, or credit line.

Title, set largest at the top left of the page: imagerender
Deck beneath it: Three kinds of picture sources — diagram scripts, chart scripts, and written prompts — are rendered into the book's figures, and a broken source is sent back for mending before it is tried again.

Hero: a print shop with three presses side by side across the middle, each a distinct small machine with its intake tray and output easel. The first, labeled mermaid, takes a sheet of spare boxes-and-arrows notation and delivers a clean flow diagram. The second, labeled R, takes a script sheet of terse code lines and delivers a graceful line chart. The third, labeled ai prompt, takes a handwritten paragraph and delivers a painted illustration. Each press's finished PNG print rests on its easel in the warm accent tone. A note above the row: each figure's little meta card names its file, its method, and what it should show; the source sheet sits beside it.

The second focus, below the presses: the mending desk. A conveyor loop runs from the presses down to a small repair desk where a clerk's lamp shines on a failed script sheet, its error slip pinned to it; a fine pen is correcting the sheet, and the loop carries it back up to its press. A note at the desk: a source that fails is mended and tried again — up to three mendings — with the error slip as the guide. A smaller side loop at the third press shows a prompt sheet being rewritten in softer words, captioned: a prompt the picture-maker refuses is rephrased once and offered again.

Two quiet details along the bottom:
- lower left: a stack of finished prints beside one dusty print with a small hourglass mark, captioned — a print newer than its source is left alone; only stale figures are re-made;
- lower right: one easel holding a plain grey sheet with small centered italic text on it, captioned — when nothing succeeds, a placeholder bearing the prompt's own words stands in, so the book builds with no hole.

One warm accent colour marks the finished prints and the mended sheet's corrections; the presses, conveyor, and desk stay in ink.
